strengths: Novel spectral analysis of diffusion frequency dynamics: The observation that low-frequency components converge early while high-frequency components resolve throughout sampling provides valuable insight, well-demonstrated through the progression map (Fig 2b) and supporting analysis.

Training-free method with strong practical value: No model retraining required; can be applied to pre-trained FLUX models, making the approach immediately deployable and reproducible by practitioners.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, FiT-v2), diverse metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, Aesthetic Score, FID, IS), systematic baselines, and human studies demonstrate thorough validation.
Well-motivated technical approach: Three principled variants (DyPE-PI, DyPE-NTK, DyPE-YaRN) logically derive from the spectral analysis with clear mathematical formulations (Eqs. 14-17).
Thorough ablation studies: Appendices D-E systematically explore design choices (scheduler variants, hyperparameter sensitivity), providing good evidence for architectural decisions.

Convincing qualitative improvements: Figures 10-13 demonstrate clear enhancement of fine details at 4096² resolution compared to existing methods, with consistent visual improvements across diverse prompts.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (Position Interpolation, NTK-aware, YaRN) are adaptations of existing language model techniques. The main novelty—time-dependent scaling κ(t)—is incremental. Lacks theoretical justification for why the exponential schedule κ(t) = λₛ · t^λₜ is optimal.

Modest quantitative improvements without statistical analysis: CLIP improvements of 6-7% (e.g., 26.64→28.43), FID improvements marginal (146.84→146.40). No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing provided, limiting confidence in result reliability.

Weak mechanistic justification: The connection between spectral progression analysis (Section 3.1) and positional embedding scaling (Section 3.2) is intuitive but not rigorously established. Why should frequency dynamics dictate positional encoding adjustments theoretically?

Limited generalization scope: Experiments only on FLUX; unclear if method transfers to other architectures (SDXL, LCM, etc.). This severely limits claims about general applicability to diffusion transformers.

Missing computational cost analysis: Claims 'no additional overhead' but provides no actual timing comparisons or memory usage data—crucial for 4096² generation assessment. Does κ(t) calculation add non-negligible cost?

Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: Method introduces hyperparameters (λₛ, λₜ, α, β). Table 5 shows significant metric variation across settings. Limited guidance for applying to new models/datasets; no robustness analysis.

Human evaluation limitations: Only 50 Aesthetic-4K prompts evaluated; preference margins (87-89%) are consistent but not overwhelming. No inter-rater agreement, disagreement analysis, or investigation of which image types benefit most.

Missing failure case and boundary analysis: No discussion of method limitations, failure modes, or whether approach extends beyond 4096² resolution. Panoramic generation (Table 8) shows marginal gains, suggesting potential method limitations.

Incomplete related work positioning: Main paper lacks comparison to recent ultra-high resolution approaches (relegated to appendix); missing discussion of patch-based and progressive generation alternatives.

Reproducibility gaps: No code availability mentioned. Missing: exact FLUX checkpoint, complete hyperparameter search ranges, runtime/memory requirements. These omissions hinder independent reproduction and comparison.

strengths: Well-motivated spectral analysis of frequency evolution during diffusion providing useful intuition about low vs high-frequency component progression
Training-free approach that works on pre-trained models without retraining or fine-tuning, which is practically valuable
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, FiT2), metrics (CLIPScore, ImageReward, Aesthetic-Score, FID), and human studies
Thorough ablation studies (Appendix D) systematically exploring design choices and scheduler variants
Clear mathematical specification of three variants (DY-PI, DY-NTK, DY-YaRN) with explicit equations
weaknesses: Incremental contribution: applying known position interpolation techniques (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) with time-dependent scaling κ(t) is a relatively straightforward extension lacking significant novelty
Unjustified design choices: the scaling function κ(t) = λ_s · t^λ_r appears ad-hoc with no principled justification for this specific functional form
Weak theoretical connection: the spectral analysis (Eq. 12) shows frequency evolution but does not rigorously justify why dynamic position scaling is the appropriate solution mechanism
Modest and inconsistent improvements: Table 1 shows many results with marginal gains (often <1 CLIPScore point). For example, DrawBench 2048×3072 DY-YaRN vs YaRN shows only 0.16 improvement

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing comparisons with progressive training, patch-based upsampling, fine-tuning as reference, and other concurrent methods; dismissive treatment of Lumina-Next relationship in Appendix B
Ambiguous novelty claim: Appendix B acknowledges time-aware position extrapolation was discussed in Zhuo et al. (2024), raising questions about what is actually novel beyond marginal modifications
Limited scope: only evaluated on text-to-image diffusion transformers; no evaluation on other resolution synthesis tasks or model architectures
Missing technical details: hyperparameter selection process for λ_s and λ_r not explained; no computational cost analysis or timing measurements; failure modes not discussed
Weak human evaluation: only 50 raters on subset of prompts; Table 2 differences within statistical noise (87-88% range) without significance testing
Insufficient theoretical grounding: no formal justification for why position encoding scaling should generalize to unseen resolutions, or how PE scaling controls frequency representation

strengths: Clear and well-motivated spectral analysis demonstrating why position extrapolation must be time-dependent: low frequencies converge early while high frequencies are resolved throughout the diffusion process
Practical training-free method that directly improves existing pre-trained models (FLUX) without retraining or additional sampling overhead

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, FiT2), multiple resolutions (2048×3072 to 4096×1365 panoramic), human evaluation (50 raters), and multiple metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, Aesthetic-Score, FID)
Elegant unification of existing position extrapolation schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) under a time-dependent scaling framework κ(t)=λ_s·t^λ_t
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 5-6) validating design choices and demonstrating the proposed exponential scheduler achieves the best balance between structural fidelity and detail preservation
Strong qualitative results with clear visual improvements in fine details, effectively demonstrated through zoom-in comparisons (Figures 3, 13) and diverse examples (Figures 10-12)
Generalizability demonstrated across multiple model variants and resolution scales, with consistent improvements
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contribution is adding time-dependence to well-known position extrapolation techniques; the building blocks (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) are existing methods
Quantitative improvements are modest at standard resolutions (e.g., CLIP improvement of 0.21 at 2048×3072: 28.43 vs 28.64), with larger gains only at ultra-high resolutions (4096+)

Theoretical justification lacks rigor: while the spectral analysis is insightful, the specific functional form κ(t)=λ_s·t^λ_t is determined empirically; no formal proof of optimality or necessity is provided
The connection between spectral evolution observations and the proposed time-dependent scaling schedule could be more formally established through optimization objectives

Limited analysis of failure modes: the severe underperformance of PI in Table 3 (FiT2) is noted but not investigated; understanding when and why dynamic scheduling helps most would strengthen the work
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is limited: ablations focus on the current setup; generalization of λ_s and λ_t choices to other models/datasets untested
Computational cost analysis is missing: while all methods are training-free, inference time comparisons between methods would provide practical utility assessment
Baseline comparisons are primarily against FLUX variants and FreeScale; broader comparison with other recent ultra-high-resolution generation methods would strengthen significance claims

strengths: Well-motivated core insight about spectral progression in diffusion processes, empirically demonstrated with clear visualization (Figure 2) showing low frequencies converge early while high frequencies develop later
Training-free approach enables immediate application to pre-trained models like FLUX without retraining or additional sampling overhead, providing significant practical advantage

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K), multiple metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, Aesthetic, FID), and extensive baseline comparisons (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN, TASR) with consistent improvements
Achieves unprecedented ultra-high resolution generation (16 megapixels at 4096×4096) on single GPU, solving critical computational bottleneck of self-attention quadratic complexity
Thorough ablation studies in appendices examining scheduler designs, hyperparameter sensitivity, and variant comparisons (Dy-PI, Dy-NTK-aware, Dy-YaRN)
Extensions to diverse applications (video generation, image editing, class-conditional generation) demonstrating robustness and generality of approach
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, logical progression from motivation through method to experiments
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why dynamic position encoding scaling specifically addresses spectral progression—connection between PE adjustment and frequency selectivity in diffusion context lacks rigorous grounding

Design choices are empirically driven without principled justification: functional form κ(t)=λ_s·t^λ_t appears arbitrary; no clear guidelines for setting hyperparameters (λ_s, λ_t, α, β) for new models/resolutions

Incomplete comparison with related high-resolution generation methods: limited quantitative comparisons with FreScale and FreeU; primarily compares against position extrapolation methods rather than other architectural approaches

Generalization and robustness concerns: evaluation heavily focused on FLUX; unclear how method generalizes to other transformer architectures, latent diffusion models, or non-transformer architectures; failure modes and fundamental limits not discussed

Evaluation limitations: some metrics (CLIP Score, ImageReward) have known reliability issues; FID unreliable at ultra-high resolutions; human evaluation limited to 20 prompts; perceptual evaluation could be more extensive

Reproducibility issues: no code release mentioned; some experimental setup details lack clarity; hyperparameter selection process not always transparent; computational overhead of frequency-aware scaling not quantified

Technical gaps in exposition: spectral analysis (Eq. 12) empirically derived without formal derivation; relationship between attention entropy and quality not explicit; abrupt transition from observations (Sec. 3.1) to method design (Sec. 3.2)
Insufficient analysis of method limitations: no discussion of fundamental resolution ceilings, when dynamic adjustment degrades performance, or sensitivity to model architecture differences
Claim of 'no additional sampling overhead' lacks support: actual computational cost of position encoding adjustments and frequency-aware scaling not provided; no inference time comparisons

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet FiT2-XL/2) with consistent metric measurements (CLIP-Score, ImageReward, Aesthetic Score, FID), demonstrating thorough empirical validation
Training-free approach requiring no retraining or additional sampling cost, making it practical for existing pre-trained diffusion models—a genuine practical contribution
Clear spectral analysis in Section 3.1 providing good intuition about how low-frequency and high-frequency components evolve differently during diffusion, with well-designed visualizations (Figure 2)
Extensive ablation studies in appendices examining scheduler designs, different PE variants, and architectural choices, showing effort toward understanding the method's behavior
Honest reporting of limitations, including mixed results on Lumina-Next and acknowledging trade-offs in panoramic generation tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution reduces to combining existing PE scaling methods (RoPE, NTK-aware, YaRN) with time-dependent scaling κ(t) = λ_t·t^λ_t, which is straightforward and incremental

Weak theoretical justification: the paper observes that frequency components evolve at different rates but fails to rigorously establish why dynamic PE scaling is the correct solution. The causal link between spectral evolution and optimal PE adjustment is assumed rather than proven

Marginal empirical improvements: Table 1 shows 1-2% improvements over baselines in many cases, and at 4096² resolution improvements are modest (26.51 vs 28.17 CLIP-Score). The method appears to mitigate degradation rather than fundamentally solve ultra-high-resolution generation

Narrow generalization scope: experiments focus primarily on FLUX with limited evaluation on other modern diffusion architectures (Stable Diffusion 3, Hunyuan, etc.). Appendix B shows poor or negative results on Lumina-Next, raising concerns about generalizability
Incomplete and inconsistent ablations: Table 6 mixes different scheduling functions without systematic comparison, and the isolated contribution of each variant (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) is unclear

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability statement despite claims of reproducibility, and hyperparameter selection for κ(t) appears empirically tuned without principled justification. The 'training-free' claim is somewhat misleading as model-specific tuning is still required

Missing theoretical bridge: the paper conflates frequency-domain spectral analysis with position-domain PE without rigorously establishing their connection or why PE scaling should track spectral progression
Lack of inference cost analysis despite per-step computation of κ(t), and missing implementation details for extending the method beyond FLUX

strengths: Novel frequency-domain analysis of diffusion spectral evolution showing differential convergence rates that motivates the dynamic positional encoding approach
Practical training-free method enabling ultra-high-resolution image generation without model retraining, immediately applicable to pre-trained models
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet, video generation, panoramic images, image editing) with consistent improvements
Well-motivated progression from frequency analysis to dynamic scaling strategies with multiple variants demonstrating generality across PE schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN)
Detailed ablation studies examining design choices and scheduler configurations with clear presentation including effective visualizations of frequency dynamics
Thorough experimental design with appropriate metrics, proper controls using same base models, and informative zoom-in comparisons showing visual quality improvements
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why exponential scaling κ(t) = λₛ·t^λₜ is optimal; connection between observed frequency evolution and the specific design appears empirically-driven rather than principled
Hyperparameter selection (λₛ, λₜ) appears somewhat arbitrary with limited guidance on choosing values for new models; sensitivity analysis incomplete despite Table 6 exploration
Modest improvements in magnitude across many metrics (often 0.1-0.3 CLIP points, negligible aesthetic gains at certain resolutions), raising questions about practical significance despite consistency
Inference-time computational cost of computing and applying κ(t) not analyzed; paper emphasizes training-free but omits timing comparisons critical for practical adoption
Lack of failure case analysis and discussion of when frequency progression assumptions may not hold; method assumes universal frequency dynamics patterns
Limited theoretical analysis of why NTK-aware variants outperform simple position interpolation and incomplete comparison with related frequency-aware methods (Lumina-Next, RIFLex)
Generalization questions: results primarily on FLUX architecture with unclear applicability to other models; no exploration of scaling beyond 4096² resolution or very different model scales
